text:
🔥 WHO DECIDES WHAT YOU EAT —
FOOD CULTURE & CULINARY HISTORY 🍽️
— The Series Index ▸ ▸ ▸  📖 Post 1 OF 26
https://t.co/tL4U46VHj1

Bread is 4,000 years older than farming. Twenty-four charred crumbs in a Jordanian fireplace broke the timeline everyone had agreed on.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

✍️ By 3 Star Media — Food Culture 🏇💨

In the Black Desert of northeastern Jordan there is a stone-lined fireplace that has not been lit in fourteen thousand four hundred years. The people who built it did not farm. They hunted gazelle, they gathered what the season gave them, and they moved. By every version of the story taught for a century, they were the ones who came before — before the fields, before the granaries, before the part of history where anything interesting happened.

In that fireplace, archaeologists found twenty-four charred crumbs. Flatbread. Made from wild einkorn and the ground tubers of a club-rush, mixed, kneaded, and baked on hot stone by people who would not see a planted field for another four millennia.

The order was wrong. Bread did not arrive because farming made grain cheap. Somebody wanted bread first, went to enormous trouble to get it, and kept doing it for four thousand years before anyone thought to make the plants come to them.

That is the shape of nearly everything in this series. The story most of us carry about food — that hunger drove invention, that invention drove progress, that progress fed the world — is not wrong so much as backward, compressed, and missing the part where somebody paid.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 THE PREMISE

We are the animal that will eat anything.

Termites show up in the hominin diet. More than 1,900 insect species are documented as edible, eaten regularly by at least two billion people. A civilization on the coast of Peru may have been built on anchovies rather than grain. A single street-food counter in Pompeii sold pig, goat, horse, fish, duck, and snail out of the same jars. The evidence for cooked food runs back roughly 780,000 years, to carp cooked at temperatures low enough that somebody was tending the fire rather than just surviving it.

And yet. Wheat, rice, and maize now supply more than half the calories humanity gets from plants, out of tens of thousands of edible species.

💡 We are the animal that will eat anything, and we ended up eating almost nothing.

This series is about how that happened, who decided it, and what each decision cost. It runs from a hearth in the Hula Valley to a school lunch tray in 2026 — through the first payroll, the first monopoly, the first restaurant, the first rating, and the first time buyers organized to define a word for themselves.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧭 THE TWO QUESTIONS

Two questions run the length of this investigation, and they turn out to be the same question wearing different clothes.

The first is who decides what is edible. Not what is nutritious — what is permitted. The camel and the hare and the pig are named in Leviticus. A Byzantine princess was condemned by a cleric for eating with a two-pronged golden instrument. The tomato sat in Europe for decades under suspicion. Insects feed at least two billion people today and are considered unthinkable by most of the other six.

The second question arrives later in history and belongs to the modern world: who decides what is good. Not safe, not filling — good. That question has an answer with a date on it, a business model behind it, and a list of people who got rich giving it.

The first question is answered, across most of this series, by whoever controls the supply. The second, it turns out, is answered the same way.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📚 WHAT'S AHEAD

🐟 POST 2 — FIRE
Carp cooked at a Levantine lakeside push the evidence for cooking back roughly 780,000 years, from a previous ceiling near 170,000.

🌾 POST 3 — THE FORAGER'S TABLE
What people ate before agriculture, and the labor it took to eat it — the chapter that makes the next one a bargain rather than a gift.

🌱 POST 4 — THE BARGAIN
Domestication happened independently in at least eleven regions and took millennia to fix a single trait in wheat; the people who farmed were measurably less healthy than the people who did not.

📜 POST 5 — GRAIN MAKES THE STATE
Barley rations recorded on clay at Lagash and Ur, down to the individual child — writing begins, in part, as food bookkeeping.

🏛️ POST 6 — THE FIRST ENTITLEMENT
Roughly a third of the free population of Rome ate on the state's account, supplied by private shipping across two thousand miles of open water, for four centuries.

🍺 POST 7 — THE BREWERS
The organism nobody saw until 1857, the monasteries that wrote down what it did, the alewives who brewed most of England's beer and lost the trade, and a rotation that fixed nitrogen a thousand years early.

🧂 POST 8 — SALT, SPICE & THE MONOPOLY
A French tax that forced every person over eight to buy salt, a march to the sea in 1930 to pick up a lump of it, and what the Dutch did to the Banda Islands in 1621 to own the world's nutmeg.

🚢 POST 9 — THE GREAT EXCHANGE
The potato and the tomato crossed one way; the best current estimate puts the death toll in the Americas at 56 million by 1600 — enough abandoned farmland returning to forest to cool the planet.

🌽 POST 10 — THE KNOWLEDGE THAT CAME WITH THE CROPS
Maize crossed the Atlantic; the alkaline process that makes it safe to live on did not — and pellagra followed the crop across two continents.

☕ POST 11 — THE STIMULANT TRADE
Two drinks with no calories in them that reorganized global trade and the working day — and the 1511 ban in Mecca aimed not at the drink but at the room.

⛓️ POST 12 — THE PRICE OF SWEETNESS
Sugarcane was domesticated in New Guinea and fed at first mainly to pigs; by 1900 sugar supplied nearly a fifth of the calories in the English diet. This chapter is the labor in between.

🥔 POST 13 — WHEN THE CROP FAILS
Ireland, and the 175-year argument over whether food exports caused the deaths — both cases given their strongest form before either is judged.

🍴 POST 14 — HOW PEOPLE ATE
Kashrut and halal as written law, Mary Douglas's famous 1966 explanation of the unclean pig and her public retraction of it thirty-six years later, and the utensil that took four centuries to become acceptable.

🏺 POST 15 — THE INVENTION OF THE RESTAURANT
Pompeii had around eighty street-food counters; Paris credits a man named Boulanger with inventing the restaurant in 1765, and the period record does not appear to contain him.

🏙️ POST 16 — MOM & POP NATION
A law written in 1882 to keep Chinese laborers out created a visa preference for merchants, and in 1915 a federal court added restaurants to the list.

🧪 POST 17 — THE STANDARD-MAKERS
Escoffier ranking a kitchen into stations, Upton Sinclair aiming at the public's heart and hitting it in the stomach, and a global food-safety system that exists because Pillsbury could not keep crumbs out of a space capsule.

⭐ POST 18 — THE RATING MACHINE
A critic's twelve friends in 1803, a tire company's 35,000 free guidebooks in 1900, and a garden shed that reached number one in London in 2017.

🍶 POST 19 — THE CRAFT THAT WASN'T WRITTEN DOWN
Escoffier wrote the kitchen down in 1903; a mold kept alive by hand for a thousand years never could be — and what that difference costs both ways.

🧊 POST 20 — THE COLD CHAIN
A prize offered by Napoleon in 1795, a method whose inventor could not explain why it worked, and the infrastructure that severed food from both the season and the place it was grown.

🧈 POST 21 — THE FAT QUESTION
A fibre-mill waste product hardened into shortening in 1911 and sold as the scientific choice; the regulator withdrew it in 2015, a hundred and four years later.

🏭 POST 22 — THE MACHINE PLATE
Nitrogen pulled from the air by a process patented in 1908 now supports an estimated 48% of the world's population — and the same chemistry is tied to 100 to 150 million deaths in twentieth-century conflict.

🌿 POST 23 — THE ORGANIC TURN
Congress defined "organic" in 1990 and the seal arrived in 2002; what the yield and nutrition evidence actually shows, and what it would take to put that food in front of 29.4 million American schoolchildren.

🗑️ POST 24 — WHAT DOESN'T GET EATEN
Roughly a third of the world's food is never eaten — about a billion meals a day — on a quarter of its farmland, while 783 million people go hungry.

🧭 POST 25 — WHO DECIDES?
Both questions, collapsed into one, and handed to the reader.

📐 POST 26 — SOURCE METHODOLOGY
Every tier, every primary source, every figure carried at reduced confidence — and the one claim that was retired outright.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 HOW TO READ THIS SERIES

Every claim here is tiered by the quality of the evidence behind it: established fact, strong evidence, plausible but unproven, genuinely disputed among qualified researchers, or not established. Where a figure comes from a single study, it is named as one. Where two bodies of evidence point opposite directions — and on organic food, they do — both are given at full strength before anything is concluded.

Three things this series will not do. It will not tell you there was a golden age of eating, because the historical record does not contain one and the people who actually cooked for a living in any century would laugh at the suggestion. It will not treat a joke, a rumor, or a panic about a cuisine as evidence about that cuisine — several chapters are specifically about what happens when somebody does. And it will not end on a verdict it has not earned across the twenty-three posts before it.

One more thing up front. A good deal of what follows is funny, in the way any story about human beings and their appetites is funny — a cleric declaring God's vengeance on a fork, a lump of cane fed to pigs that reorganized three continents, an empire trading Manhattan for a nutmeg island. There are also chapters where nothing is funny at all, and this series does not go looking for jokes in them.

🐟 Next: a lakeside in the Levant, a hearth, and two species of carp that push the history of cooking back by more than half a million years — along with the reason a controlled fire, not a sharp stone, is the technology everything else in this story is built on.

📖 Post 1 of 26

🇬🇲🇬🇲: Darboe leader of the United Democratic Party, used a rally in Allunhari in the Upper River Region to tell younger Gambians that the 5 December 2026 presidential election belongs to them more than to the generation that fought earlier political battles. He said veterans such as Alagie Nfamara Jabbie and Mba Sillah had already done their part, and that people in their twenties, thirties and forties now carry the responsibility of deciding whether the country moves toward what he called progress or stays on a path of economic hardship. He asked them to convert that responsibility into votes for the UDP.

The speech turned on the cost of living, especially rice. Darboe recalled a 1996 meeting in Garawol at which he warned that electing Yahya Jammeh could push a bag of rice from about 250 dalasis toward 500. He said some voters dismissed that as opposition talk, only for prices later to rise far beyond the warning. He then argued that a later government promised to cut the price from 1,500 dalasis to 750, yet consumers now face figures he put between 2,000 and 3,000. The comparison was meant to tell voters to measure political promises against what they actually pay.

Darboe also opposed another term for President Adama Barrow, saying a third administration would deepen economic and governance problems. He accused the government of neglecting hospitals and farmers while spending on vehicles, workshops and conferences, and warned that five more years would further weaken agriculture, on which many Gambians depend. The remarks sit inside a wider UDP effort to mobilize the Upper River Region ahead of a first-past-the-post presidential contest in which Barrow is seeking a third term and Darboe is the principal opposition challenger. Coalition talks among opposition parties have been difficult, and the UDP has urged other forces to gather behind it rather than a separately selected independent candidate.

The rice history is campaign rhetoric rather than a full economic record. Rice in The Gambia is largely imported, so exchange rates, world prices, freight and policy all matter. Darboe’s story tracks a long rise in nominal prices, but it is offered as a political test, not an official price series.

text:
The small chops economy

The last party I attended was the wedding of a colleague's daughter, and before I arrived, I had already made a firm decision that I was not going to eat small chops. I know myself well enough to know that small chops is one of my major weaknesses, and with my current attempt to eat better, I was not interested in testing my willpower against warm puff-puff, samosa, spring rolls and peppered chicken when I already knew how that contest was likely to end.

So when the food came around, I quickly settled for a small portion of amala, gbegiri and ewedu. It was strategic; if I ate something early enough, then by the time the small chops began making its way around the hall, I would hopefully be full enough to decline it without feeling deprived. It worked, and I left the party rather pleased with myself, although watching those trays move around the room made me wonder how many other people had arrived that afternoon with equally good intentions, only to find those intentions becoming considerably less important when the small chops appeared.

There is something about the arrival of small chops at a Lagos party that brightens people's faces, and I have watched it happen too many times to think it is accidental. No matter how engrossed everyone appears in conversation, the appearance of a tray somewhere in the room attracts a certain quiet attention. People continue talking, occasionally glance at their phones and generally maintain the appropriate level of sophistication, while somehow remaining completely aware of the waiter's location and whether there will be any portions left by the time he reaches them.

Then there is that first bite of puff-puff, particularly when it is warm, soft inside, slightly crisp outside and sweet without being overwhelmingly so, which brings an amount of pleasure completely disproportionate to its size. I suspect this is also why small chops has been the downfall of many a fit-fam journey, because we don't quite treat it as proper food and therefore don't always account for it as such.

A plate of jollof rice is a commitment, and amala, gbegiri and ewedu certainly require you to acknowledge that you have eaten, but small chops allows us a degree of plausible deniability. One puff-puff hardly feels consequential, the samosa is small, the spring roll even narrower, and the peppered snail disappears quickly enough for you to convince yourself that nothing substantial has happened. By the waiter's third visit, you may have consumed far more than you intended while remaining quite sincere in the belief that you did not really eat at the party.

Small chops also occupies a useful middle ground in Lagos social life, somewhere between "I am too sophisticated to sit down with a full plate of rice" and "i don't want to appear rude by refusing the host's hospitality". You can take a few pieces, continue your conversation, preserve most of your lipstick and dignity, and avoid having to negotiate a large piece of goat meat while dressed in your finest aso-ebi.

Then, of course, there is the theatre, because somewhere along the evolution of Lagos parties, merely serving small chops apparently stopped being enough. What once arrived quietly on a waiter's tray can now be accompanied by music, dancing servers, smoke, sparklers and elaborate serving contraptions, with enough choreography to momentarily distract attention from the celebrants themselves, particularly if the likes of skewered ram or goat is a part of the entourage. I have watched entire halls turn towards these processions, phones raised to record the spectacle, as the servers dance their way between tables.

There is something wonderfully excessive about it, but it also feels completely at home in Lagos, where we have become particularly good at turning the smallest elements of a celebration into an experience. Beneath all the fanfare is also something quite familiar about us, because whether it is a wedding, birthday, naming ceremony, corporate event or government function, feeding people remains part of our language of hospitality, while accepting what is offered is one of the small ways we acknowledge it.

Small chops has adapted itself perfectly to that exchange, being informal enough not to interrupt a conversation, substantial enough for a host to feel that something has been offered, small enough for those of us watching our weight to negotiate with our conscience, and frivolous enough to make people genuinely happy when they see it coming.

I managed to resist it at my colleague's daughter's wedding, helped considerably by the strategic intervention of the ever faithful amala, but I am under no illusion that this represents a permanent victory, because there will always be another Lagos party, another tray making its way across the room and another moment when the smell of warm puff-puff makes all the promises made before leaving home suddenly require fresh consideration.

text:
G’mar Tov! 

Tzom Gedaliah falls at dawn tomorrow, Monday 14 September 2026 / 3 Tishrei 5787, from sunrise until nightfall. 

After Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE and carried most of Judah into exile, he left a poor remnant in the land as farmers and appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, grandson of Shaphan, as governor. Gedaliah set up at Mizpah, welcomed refugees who had fled to Ammon, Moab, and Edom, and tried to rebuild a quiet life under Babylon. His family had protected the prophet Jeremiah, and he preached the same counsel: accept the yoke, stay in the land, plant and harvest. 

For a brief moment it looked as if Jewish life in Eretz Yisrael might survive the catastrophe.

That hope ended in the seventh month. Ishmael son of Nethaniah, of royal Davidic blood and backed by Baalis king of Ammon, came to Mizpah with ten men. Johanan son of Kareah had already warned Gedaliah of the plot and even offered to kill Ishmael first. Gedaliah refused to believe a fellow Jew would do it and hosted them at a meal. They rose from the table and murdered him, the Jews with him, and the Babylonian garrison. The next day they slaughtered eighty pilgrims coming from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria with offerings. Johanan rescued some of the captives, but Ishmael escaped to Ammon. Terrified of Babylonian revenge, the last remnant ignored Jeremiah’s plea and fled to Egypt, dragging the prophet with them. The land was left empty. Tradition treats this as the last ember of Jewish autonomy going out, and the Sages said the death of a righteous leader is like the burning of the House of the Almighty. 

Zechariah already knew it as “the fast of the seventh month.” Some say Gedaliah was killed on 1 Tishrei and the fast was pushed to the third so it would not fall on Rosh Hashanah; if the third is Shabbat the fast moves to Sunday. That is why we fast tomorrow: not only for one man’s blood, but for the civil strife that finished the exile.

Seal of Gedaliah

It's not mocking to point out the truth.  Calvinism is one of many mostly mid- and late 20th century cults, each of which has some commonalities:
- They have a founder that has new revelations or interpretations. (In Calvinism's case, that's John Calvin.)
- They have additional writings that clarify those new revelations, because those revelations don't appear in scripture. (In Calvinism's case, that's the Confessions.)
- They believe that every other Christian cult and it’s leader are wrong, but their personal cult leader is right, and their cult is different.
- They elevate their new revelation to the level of the gospel itself, making an idol of the system.
- Their fundamental belief systems are often gnostic in nature -- they have to be deduced from scripture -- and they rely on taking things out of their original context.  (In Calvinism's case, Ephesians 1 and Romans 9 stand out as two passages that don't mean what Calvinists declare, and they use only specific verses to defend those points, even when the rest of the surrounding text contradicts those interpretations.)
- There's always something additional beyond simple belief required for salvation (In Calvinism, this is God's selection.)
- They must ignore or re-interpret scripture that contradicts their view. (Too many to name in Calvinism's case!  All of scripture expects man to have choices and a responsibility to make them.)
- They get "bonus prizes!" Eternal fellowship with God is a BIG deal, but to attract new converts to a cult, you've got to offer something else.  (In Calvinism's case, it's the notion that you're special and selected, not like the rest of the dregs of humanity.)

Other similar Christian cults:
- Islam
- Jehovah's Witnesses
- Mormonism
- Branch Davidians
- The People's Temple
- Seventh Day Adventists
- Etc.

10. Possessions and “sell all”

Kingdom / Acts 1–8: sell that ye have and give alms (Luke 12:33). Sell all that thou hast… and thou shalt have treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21; Luke 18:22). All that believed had all things common (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–35). Ananias and Sapphira judged for holding back (Acts 5).

Paul: charge them that are rich… that they do good, ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Let every man give as he purposeth in his heart (2 Corinthians 9:7). Work with your own hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

11. The commissions

Matthew 28 / Mark 16 / Luke 24 / Acts 1: teach all nations, baptizing them. Signs following. Begin at Jerusalem. The Twelve sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28). This is the kingdom commission. Interrupted by Israel’s fall. Resumes after the Body is caught up.

Paul’s commission: make all men see the fellowship of the mystery (Ephesians 3:9). Ambassador of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). Gospel of the uncircumcision committed to him (Galatians 2:7). Not sent to baptize (1 Corinthians 1:17).

12. Hebrews through Revelation

Assigned to believing Israel / the little flock / tribulation saints, not the Body.
•Hebrews — last days (1:2), signs of them that heard Him (2:3–4), new covenant with the house of Israel (8:8–10), falling away, no more sacrifice, a city to come.
•James — twelve tribes, faith + works, last days, anointing with oil.
•1–2 Peter — scattered strangers of the dispersion, baptism saves, fiery trial, day of the Lord.
•1–3 John — antichrist, last time, commandment-keeping as the test, sin unto death.
•Jude — contend for the faith once delivered, Enoch prophecy.
•Revelation — Jewish temple, tribes, 144,000, two witnesses, wrath, overcomers, millennial kingdom on earth.

Paul never writes the Body into Daniel’s seventieth week, the day of the Lord wrath, or Israel’s new covenant priesthood.

13. Acts 1–8 (still kingdom)

Acts 1 — “wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?” Acts 2 — Joel’s last days to Israel; “to you, and to your children.” Acts 3 — repent so the Messiah can return and the times of restitution come. Acts 7 — Stephen’s appeal; Israel resists the Holy Ghost; the prophetic offer is rejected. Acts 8 — Samaria (still Acts 1:8 order); apostles from Jerusalem must lay on hands.
Paul is not yet converted. The mystery Body is not on the page yet.

How the “contradictions” are handled

They are only contradictions if you:

1. Start the Body of Christ in Acts 2

2. Make Jesus’ earthly words your mail

3. Put James / Hebrews / 1 John on the same doctrinal footing as Romans / Ephesians

4. Preach Acts 2:38 as the gospel for today

Rightly divided: God changed programs after Israel’s fall and Paul’s conversion. Scripture does not fight itself. Men mix what God divided.

Here is another way to break it down:

1
Kingdom: “The kingdom is at hand.” (Matt 4:17)
 Paul: “Christ died for our sins… and rose again.” (1 Cor 15:3-4)

2
Kingdom: Spoken since the world began. (Acts 3:21)
 Paul: Kept secret since the world began. (Rom 16:25)

3
Kingdom: To Israel first. (Matt 10:5-6)
 Paul: To all without difference. (Rom 10:12)

4
Kingdom: Believe Jesus is the Christ. (John 20:31)
 Paul: Believe the finished work of the cross. (Eph 1:13)

5
Kingdom: Repent and be baptized for remission. (Acts 2:38)
 Paul: Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel. (1 Cor 1:17)

6
Kingdom: He that endureth to the end shall be saved. (Matt 24:13)
 Paul: Sealed unto the day of redemption. (Eph 4:30)

7
Kingdom: Faith without works is dead. (James 2:24)
 Paul: To him that worketh not, but believeth. (Rom 4:5)

8
Kingdom: Keep the commandments. (Matt 19:17)
 Paul: Ye are not under the law, but under grace. (Rom 6:14)

Cont..

text:
In a statement issued on September 11, Human Rights Watch (HRW) warned that the wave of pre-election violence "risks plunging Kenya back into the pattern of human rights violations seen in past elections." Incidents documented by HRW include a machete attack on a church in Kisumu in July that left one person dead; an attack on an opposition convoy in Homa Bay in August that killed three people and injured journalists; and the shooting of Siaya Governor Orengo’s convoy in Migori on August 30. Amnesty International went further, alleging "state-sponsored acts of terror" during the Ol-Kalou by-election, citing incidents such as masked gunmen opening fire at polling stations, targeted attacks on journalists, and the violent dispersal of voters.

**The Ruto Administration’s Response and Controversy**

Last week, President Ruto announced a fund of nearly $15 million to compensate approximately 2,000 documented victims of protest-related human rights violations occurring between 2017 and 2025. Ruto stated that the compensation was "not a price tag on life, pain, or loss" and should not be viewed as a reward for violence or criminal activity. However, human rights organizations rejected the compensation scheme, pointing out that it excluded certain victims, offered insufficient payouts, and lacked transparency. Meanwhile, Ruto insisted that "anyone mobilized to destroy property or sow chaos" would not be tolerated.

**Shadows Looming Over 2027**

Kenya’s general election is scheduled for August 10, 2027, and Ruto is expected to seek re-election. Yet, a pattern of pre-election violence is emerging: armed attacks on opposition rallies, assaults on journalists and human rights defenders, and allegations of excessive force by security forces. Data from Amnesty International and Odipo Dev indicate that 453 protest events were recorded in the first half of 2026—a 29% increase compared to the same period the previous year. Human rights groups warn that if the government continues to condone the normalization of violence, public confidence in democratic institutions will completely erode. Sifuna’s rally represents a political response to this trend—an attempt by the opposition to demonstrate that peaceful mobilization remains possible, even under the shadow of violence.

text:
#Breaking Aidan “Turtleboy” Kearney published the name, face, and city of the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Saturday night.
#massachusetts

Doxxing and allegedly intimidating jurors and witnesses appears to be a pattern for Kearney who has faced legal trouble for his previous alleged actions - and could face legal consequences for his latest dox.

#trial
🔸️In fact, Kearney wrote that in 2023 he “named and shamed the lone holdout juror from the Michael Chesna murder trial who refused to deliberate on an 11-1 guilty vote and caused a mistrial.”

🔸️Juror Doe’s 2024 affidavit quoted Kearney saying he found that holdout and “shamed her, as I should, cause it’s shameful.”

🔸️And he doxxed the jury foreman in the Karen Read’s first trial.
According to an affidavit by a juror in that trial, Kearney claimed to know the foreman’s name, home, and job.

He scared the jurors so much that they filed motions with the court asking Judge Beverly Cannone to indefinitely seal that jury list - which she did.

➡️It quoted Kearney demanding the name of the “idiot on this jury” who would not return the not-guilty verdict he wanted and saying whoever did that “subverted justice” and “helped cover up for a murder.”

But it gets worse, Kearney ran the “Canton Coverup” series on the Karen Read case in Canton and Dedham, landing him a grand jury indictment on:

🔷️Eight counts of witness intimidation,
🔷️Five counts of picketing a witness, and
🔷️Three counts of conspiracy.

In that series, he named alleged targets and allegedly caused a disruption at D&E Pizza, tied to one of the families he was charged with intimidating.
Kearney has pleaded not guilty and calls it journalism.

But according to court documents:

➡️Kearney named witnesses,
➡️Published addresses and phone numbers,
➡️Led a July 22, 2023, Rolling Road Rally that stopped at witnesses’ houses with a bullhorn.
➡️He confronted people in public, including at a high-school lacrosse game, and
➡️Coordinated with Read’s camp.
➡️On video outside one of the family's homes, he told neighbors “Cop ki*lers” lived there.
➡️He told one of the family members that he allegedly harassed that he did not have “the right to live peacefully.”
➡️And he admitted publicly that his actions were to affect the jury pool. - again all according to court documents and all are allegations.

His pending charges:
🔺️Two Norfolk witness-intimidation dockets remain open
🔺️One related docket was dropped in October 2025 after the office was left without a prosecutor
🔺️Kearney was acquitted in 2025 of a restraining-order violation tied to an ex-girlfriend at a Read hearing.
🔺️An Atlantic County, New Jersey, grand jury indicted him in July 2026 on a cyber-harassment count.
🔺️In April 2026, four witnesses in the Karen Read trial sued both Read and Kearney for defamation and civil conspiracy.

This is the third time he has doxxed a juror in a Massachusetts m*rder trial.
Kearney posted the name of the juror (which I will not post) and his picture.

He identifies him as the lone holdout in the Clancy case, detailed how he was “arrested for assaulting his ex-wife,” later “beat up his minor nephew,” and “now lives in (a city I won't name) in an apartment where he is refusing to pay rent for the last 6 months.”

But he goes further making accusations against the juror by posting:

"This is exactly what happened btw. Lady got strangled and beat up. Then 5 years later every conserva-bro on Twitter is calling him a “patriot” and “hero.” I’d reach out to the media too."

"This juror is a piece of sh*t, woman abusing, kid abusing, deadbeat squatter. He didn’t holdup that jury cuz he’s a man of conviction. He’s just a combative, argumentative, a**hole."

text:
NASDAQ FUTURES ARE DOWN 1.20% TONIGHT. DOW FUTURES ARE DOWN 0.10%. READ THE GAP:

Nasdaq-100 futures at 29,034.75, -352.00 pts / -1.20%. Dow futures at 52,532.00, -53.00 pts / -0.10%. S&P 500 futures at 7,623.00, -36.50 pts / -0.48%. Russell 2000 futures at 2,899.50, -5.00 pts / -0.17%. Futures are bets on where an index finishes later - at nine on a Sunday evening, the only live opinion on Monday's US open.

The verdict: money is leaving one corner of the market, not the market. Real fear drags everything down together. A technology index down more than a full point while the Dow is down a tenth, and small companies less than that, is a swap - and Tokyo, an hour into its session, is making the same one.

The Nikkei 225 sits at 63,276, -735 pts / -1.15%, on top of Friday's close of 64,011 after a 1.93% fall. Friday's decline in Tokyo was not broad either. SoftBank Group fell 12%, Kioxia Holdings 8.6%, Advantest 4.5%, Tokyo Electron 2.6%. Every one of those either makes something the AI build needs or bankrolls the people who do.

Hong Kong and Shanghai open at 9:30am local, about half an hour from now; their last settled levels are Friday's - the Hang Seng at 24,806, -149 pts / -0.60%, the Shanghai Composite at 3,888.11, -46.29 pts / -1.18%. Europe is shut until early tomorrow, and Friday left it pointing the other way: the FTSE 100 at 10,650, +41.54 pts / +0.39%; Germany's DAX at 25,569, +207 pts / +0.82%; France's CAC 40 at 8,179.77, +63.01 pts / +0.78%. Those are heavy in oil producers, banks and insurers; Asia's in chipmakers. That is most of the difference.

What changed over the weekend was not a number. On Saturday, September 12, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published a roughly 3,800-word essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing his own industry should slow down: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman agreed; Elon Musk wrote "Dario is right." Neither company is listed, so neither is something an ordinary investor can own. The spending plans built on them are.

Arm Holdings $ARM at $253.60 (overnight), -$11.19 / -4.23% from Friday's $264.79 close. The Cambridge, England company, 9,584 employees, makes no chips. It designs the processor blueprints, licenses them out, and collects a royalty on nearly every chip built to one - most of the phones on earth, and a growing slice of data-center hardware. Tonight's price sits 54 cents above Friday's intraday low of $253.06, so the whole of Friday has been handed back before New York wakes up.

The wire to Tokyo is literal: SoftBank Group, the Nikkei name that fell 12% on Friday, owns about 87% of Arm. And the price is the most future-dated around - roughly 272 times the last year of profit, on $283B of market value. Nobody pays that for this year's royalties; they pay it for royalties on chips nobody has designed yet. A weekend spent asking the industry to slow down lands there first.

That same number keeps Arm off all six Len5es. The Growth Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and 272 times has charged for years of it in advance; Hypergrowth wants a business early as well as fast, and a company founded in 1990 with 9,584 staff is not early; Quality-Value wants a business almost nobody could rebuild bought under what it is worth, and nobody is rebuilding this one but there is no discount on offer. CHANGE IT: a real fall in the shares with the royalty stream intact, which would put it in front of the value styles for the first time - it is already 44.0% under June 18's $452.70.

The other half of the swap: Chevron at $216.78 (overnight), +$2.72 / +1.27% from Friday's $214.06 close - and the Houston company's best price in a year, $217.40, was set on Thursday, September 10. An oil major within 0.3% of a one-year high on the same night a chip designer gives back a full session is the argument in one pair of quotes. Crude has been dearer since Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline last week: revenue in Houston, a cost nearly everywhere else. Chevron is on none of the six Len5es either - the 3.3% dividend is paid out of its own cash, but the earnings behind it move with a barrel price the company does not set, and that swing is what the Income Len5 exists to avoid.

One correction to the tidy version: Tokyo is not simply echoing New York. Japan has its own appointment. The Bank of Japan meets Thursday and Friday, September 17 and 18, and surveys and rate futures put the chance of a lift to 1.25% from 1.00% between 88% and 97% - a level Japan has not seen since April 1995. The case is domestic: real wages, meaning pay once inflation is subtracted, rose 2.4% in July from a year earlier on the labour ministry's survey, the fastest since 2021. The yen has firmed to around 152-153 per dollar from nearer 164 over the past year, and a stronger yen shrinks what a Japanese exporter's overseas sales are worth once converted home. Two reasons to sell tonight, not one.

Two dates settle it, and neither is in Asia. The Federal Reserve announces Wednesday, September 16, with its target range at 3.50%-3.75% since December 2025 and futures putting the chance of an increase near 80% to 90%. The Bank of Japan follows on Friday. Until then the figure to watch is not the Nasdaq one - it is the distance between it and the Dow one. If Dow and Russell futures are still within a couple of tenths of flat at the 9:30am ET open, tonight was a swap between kinds of stock. If they fall in behind the Nasdaq, it was people stepping back from shares generally. One caution either way: far fewer people trade at nine on a Sunday than at ten on a Monday, and overnight gaps fade by the US open more often than they hold.

Nothing this weekend made anyone want to own fewer shares. It made them want to own different ones. Two central banks answer this week, one on Wednesday and one on Friday, and neither of them will be replying to an essay.

Not investment advice.

text:
A 12-seat electric boat just flew above the ocean.

A balloon travelled 30,000km and delivered mobile service to ordinary phones from the stratosphere.

And scientists may be able to detect schizophrenia through subtle patterns in speech.

1/12

Here is your weekly science and technology roundup 🧵👇

2/12

Regent Craft’s Seaglider just completed its maiden crewed flight over Narragansett Bay.

It starts as a boat, rises onto hydrofoils, then flies just above the water using ground effect.

Two people took part in the 30-second test.

The company wants it to become a new kind of electric coastal transport, with proposed routes linking places like New York, Boston, Miami, and nearby destinations.

3/12

The clever bit is ground effect.

Flying very close to the water creates a cushion of air beneath the wings, helping the vehicle travel more efficiently than a conventional aircraft.

It is not quite a plane.

Not quite a boat.

But if it scales, it could make short coastal trips much faster without needing an airport.

4/12

Scientists are also finding that AI may spot signs of schizophrenia before doctors can.

Models analysing vocal features and the flow of speech reportedly distinguished people with schizophrenia from healthy controls with up to 87% accuracy.

That is not a diagnosis tool yet.

But when people with psychotic disorders can wait an average of 18 months for diagnosis, earlier warning could matter a lot.

5/12

The important word is support.

An AI model might one day help clinicians notice patterns worth investigating sooner.

It should not be making life-changing calls on its own.

Mental-health care needs context, clinical judgement, consent, and people involved at every step.

6/12

Researchers completed the most detailed biological study yet of Maria Branyas, who lived beyond 117.

Her body showed classic signs of ageing in her immune system and chromosomes.

But she also had low inflammation, protective genetic traits, and markers suggesting a biological age younger than her calendar age.

Ageing is clearly not one single process.

7/12

The study may also help researchers understand blood cancers linked to ageing.

That is the promise of looking at one person through multiple biological layers at once:

Genes, immune function, inflammation, and cellular changes can tell a much richer story than a birthday ever could.

8/12

Sceye sent an unmanned stratospheric platform from New Mexico to Japan and back.

The round trip covered 30,000km over 30 days.

For a week, it provided mobile broadband, drone communications, and edge computing from high above the Earth.

Working with SoftBank, it supported voice calls, texts, and video streaming to regular, unmodified phones.

9/12

That makes stratospheric infrastructure worth watching.

Satellites are powerful but expensive and complex.

A high-altitude platform could offer another way to extend connectivity, especially for future 6G networks or areas with weak ground infrastructure.

The sky between cell towers and space may become valuable real estate.

10/12

A major medical breakthrough this week:

The FDA approved Orzeyful for type 1 narcolepsy.

The pill mimics orexin, a brain chemical missing in people with the condition.

In late-stage trials, patients stayed awake for more than 20 minutes in controlled tests, compared with four to five minutes before treatment.

That is more than two decades of research turning into a real option for patients.

11/12

Scientists may have found a better route to snake antivenom too.

They combined toxin-blocking proteins that rattlesnakes naturally use to avoid being harmed by their own venom.

In lab tests, the mixture was about 10 times more potent than current commercial antivenom and neutralised venom from other viper species too.

It could eventually mean cheaper treatments made without relying on horses or sheep.

12/12

And a few science rabbit holes doing the rounds:

• A yellow sponge and pink sea star spotted more than a mile beneath the Atlantic look suspiciously like SpongeBob and Patrick
• An ancient rhino relative called Elasmotherium looked remarkably unicorn-like
• Someone connected a PS5 to a black-and-white TV from 1949
• A viral fake London Underground notice is roasting smart-glasses wearers
• A major study on morning coffee is generating plenty of discussion
The future is not arriving in one place.
It is lifting off from the water, floating in the stratosphere, hiding in the bloodstream, and occasionally looking like SpongeBob on the ocean floor.

text:
Seven. Zero. Seventy. 70. 

For 44 years, the claim has been repeated that Georgia was so consumed by antisemitism after the 1915 lynching of Leo Frank that half of the state’s Jewish population fled.

Yet the historical support offered for that sweeping assertion amounts to seventy separate claims, repeated across books, articles, lectures, documentaries, and legal filings, without adequate documentary evidence to establish the central proposition.

That is seventy iterations of the same anti-Southern, anti-Georgian, and anti-Gentile narrative: that the August 17, 1915 lynching of Leo Frank triggered an exodus of roughly half of Georgia’s Jewish population because the state had become intolerably antisemitic.

The claim has traveled far beyond popular retellings. The Anti-Defamation League of B’nai B’rith, @ADL, has repeated it in filings at the U.S. Supreme Court. 

But repetition, even in prominent institutions and legal documents, is not proof. The question is not how often the allegation has been made. The question is whether contemporaneous population records, migration data, synagogue membership rolls, city directories, census figures, and Jewish communal records actually substantiate it.

So far, the claim’s frequency appears to exceed its evidence.

text:
70 Examples of the State-wide Fearmongering Persecution Hoax About a Supposed Jewish Exodus Out of Georgia in the Aftermath of the Leo Frank Case

March 7, 1982, The Tennessean, Sandra Roberts, “13 Words Shook History.”

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state in the months following the Leo Frank lynching. This is the earliest quantitative version I have located so far that combines the two numbers that later become standard: a total Jewish population of 3,000 and approximately one-half supposedly leaving Georgia. The article did not identify a statewide migration study, census of Jewish departures, synagogue survey, or other demographic source for the number.

March 8, 1982, The New York Times, Wendell Rawls Jr.

Version: about half the 3,000 Jews in Georgia left the state in the aftermath. This appeared one day after The Tennessean version and uses almost the same numerical formula. The wording softens “half” to “about half,” but the population base remains 3,000. Later sources and legal briefs would cite or rely on this New York Times article, giving the figure a much more authoritative appearance.

March 9, 1982, Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

Version: about half the state’s 3,000 Jews reportedly moved away. This appeared only two days after The Tennessean and one day after The New York Times. The word “reportedly” is worth noticing because it signals that JTA was passing along a report rather than presenting its own demographic research. The same basic 3,000 and one-half formula continued.

March 25, 1982, Rhode Island Jewish Voice & Herald.

Version: about half the state’s 3,000 Jews reportedly moved away. This was essentially the JTA version carried into another publication. It is therefore another published appearance, but it is not another independent demographic investigation. It shows how quickly the numerical formula was already moving through syndicated Jewish press reporting.

April 9, 1982, The Voice of Miami, Father John B. Sheerin.

Version: half the 3,000 Jews in Georgia left the state. By this point the number had moved beyond the original Tennessee and national newspaper reports into commentary. The qualification “about” disappears again, leaving the cleaner and stronger formula of half of 3,000. No separate demographic accounting was identified with the assertion.

December 27, 1983, Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

Version: about 1,500 of the 3,000 Jews in Georgia fled. Here the arithmetic that had previously been left to the reader becomes explicit. Half of 3,000 is converted into 1,500 people, and “moved away” becomes the stronger word “fled.” This is an early example of the story becoming more definite as it is repeated.

March 1984, AJR Information.

Version: about half the 3,000 Jews of Georgia fled the state. The same population base, fraction, and flight language appear again. By now the formula had crossed from American newspapers into another Jewish historical publication. The wording reads like an established historical statistic even though the underlying statewide departure count is still not supplied.

March 12, 1986, Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

Version: about 1,500 of Georgia’s Jewish population of 3,000 fled. This repeats the explicit arithmetic seen in the 1983 JTA version. The population is presented as 3,000, the alleged departures as 1,500, and the movement is described as flight. This formulation would become one of the easiest versions for later writers to repeat because both the numerator and denominator are already supplied.

1988, Athan G. Theoharis and John Stuart Cox, The Boss.

Version: about half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews fled the state. The numerical story had now entered book-length historical writing. Once a newspaper assertion appears in a scholarly or historical book, later writers can encounter the figure without ever seeing where it originated. This is one route by which a recent numerical assertion can acquire an older historical appearance.

February 1, 1994, Helen Schneider Silver, The Jewish Traveler.

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews fled the state. Again, the qualification “about” disappears. The statement gives readers a definite population and a definite proportion, but not the records used to calculate either the departures or the supposed post-lynching loss.

December 1, 1998, Jay Robert Nash, Terrorism in the 20th Century.

Version: Jews by the thousands departed Atlanta. This is a major change in both geography and scale. The earlier story involved roughly 1,500 people leaving the entire State of Georgia. Here the language shifts to Atlanta and expands the departure figure into the plural “thousands.”

March 18, 2004, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Kay Powell.

Version: half of Atlanta’s Jews moved away. Georgia has now become Atlanta. The original statewide formula is transformed into a city-level assertion, even though those are not interchangeable populations. This is an example of the geography changing while the one-half fraction survives.

Circa 2008, archived Wikipedia, “Leo Frank.”

Version: approximately half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. Wikipedia helped give the formula enormous online reach. The familiar components remain intact: approximately 3,000 Jews, approximately one-half leaving, and Georgia as the geographic unit. Once placed in Wikipedia, the wording became particularly easy for websites, students, journalists, and later authors to repeat.

November 13, 2009, HISTORY.

Version: thousands of Jewish residents in Atlanta were forced to flee the city. This version changes the scale and the location. Instead of approximately 1,500 leaving Georgia, readers are told that thousands fled Atlanta, and “were forced to flee” adds an even stronger causal element.

April 27, 2010, Jewish Currents, Lawrence Bush.

Version: about half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left in connection with the aftermath. The original numerical formula remains recognizable almost three decades after its 1982 appearance. The population base and fraction survive with little alteration.

August 17, 2010, Poe Forward.

Version: approximately half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This closely resembles the Wikipedia formulation. It shows the numerical story spreading through internet historical writing, where repetition can occur without any new demographic research being performed.

September 12, 2011, Marietta Patch, Todd Hudson.

Version: nearly half of Georgia’s Jewish population is said to have left the state. The exact 3,000 figure disappears, but the one-half proportion remains. The phrase “is said to have” is also revealing because it acknowledges that the writer is repeating an inherited account.

May 27, 2013, Times of Israel, Matt Lebovic.

Version: half of the state’s Jews fled Georgia. The 3,000 denominator drops out completely. What remains is the dramatic half-of-an-entire-population statement. A reader encountering only this version would have no indication where the fraction originated.

August 23, 2013, The Jewish Standard.

Version: about half the 3,000 Jews living in Georgia soon moved out of state. This returns almost exactly to the 1982 numerical structure. The 3,000 population, one-half fraction, and statewide departure remain intact more than thirty years later.

2013, The Jewish Community of North Alabama: A Brief History.

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. The number had entered regional Jewish historical writing. Again, it appears as a straightforward demographic statement rather than as an unresolved or disputed estimate.

September 25, 2013, Arden Theatre, Sally Ollove.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled the state. The denominator disappears, but the half-population assertion remains. This is another route of transmission, moving the story into theatrical and educational background material connected with presentations of the Leo Frank story.

May 2014, Jacqueline S. May dissertation.

Version: approximately half of the state’s Jewish population left the area. The assertion now appears in academic work. The wording becomes less geographically precise with “left the area,” but the approximately-one-half proportion remains.

August 18, 2015, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Greg Bluestein.

Version: as many as half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews fled. “As many as” introduces a qualification, but the old 3,000 denominator remains. This appeared during the centennial coverage of Frank’s 1915 lynching, bringing the numerical story before a new generation of readers.

August 21, 2015, JWeekly, Seth Brysk.

Version: half of Atlanta’s Jewish community fled the state. Once again, Atlanta replaces Georgia as the population being divided in half. The destination language remains statewide because the community supposedly fled the state, creating a hybrid Atlanta-to-Georgia version.

September 21, 2015, ADL Philadelphia, Nancy K. Baron-Baer.

Version: half of Atlanta’s Jewish community fled the state. This repeats the Atlanta formulation. The significance here is institutional transmission. The numerical story was no longer confined to historical articles or books but was being repeated by a major advocacy organization.

September 25, 2015, Vindicator, Nancy K. Baron-Baer reprint.

Version: the same half of Atlanta’s Jewish community fled the state formulation. This is a direct example of republication rather than independent confirmation. One source generates another visible appearance of the same numerical story.

Circa 2016, Lorne Bair Rare Books.

Version: as many as half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This restores the statewide 3,000 formula. The numerical assertion had spread even into antiquarian book descriptions and historical sales material.

February 6, 2017, ADL brief in Washington v. Trump.

Version: antisemitic violence surrounding the Frank episode caused about half of Georgia’s Jewish population to flee. This represents an important new stage because the assertion entered federal litigation. The wording was no longer simply appearing in journalism or historical commentary. It was being presented to a federal court as historical background.

February 8, 2017, ADL brief in Aziz v. Trump.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population was driven to flee. The wording closely follows the other ADL filing. This is another documentary appearance, but not another demographic study. The same historical assertion was being reused across separate cases.

February 14, 2017, ADL filing in Darweesh v. Trump.

Version: again, about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. The repetition across litigation illustrates how one historical sentence can multiply into numerous official-looking citations simply because substantially the same brief language is filed in several courts.

March 3, 2017, ADL/JCPA filing in IRAP v. Trump.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. The same historical example continued through litigation challenging the Trump administration’s travel restrictions. No new Georgia demographic calculation accompanied the new filing.

March 14, 2017, ADL and allied organizations in Hawaii v. Trump.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. The geographical and proportional formula remains unchanged. Another court filing therefore becomes another published documentary appearance of the same inherited statistic.

April 19, 2017, ADL and allied organizations, IRAP v. Trump, Fourth Circuit.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. 

The assertion moved upward into federal appellate litigation. Its appearance in a higher court did not turn it into a new demographic study, but it gave the sentence another authoritative legal setting.

April 21, 2017, ADL and allied organizations, Hawaii v. Trump, Ninth Circuit.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. This is another near-identical use in a separate federal appellate proceeding. The historical assertion was effectively being copied through a family of related briefs.

September 2, 2017, Neil Silberblatt, online review.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left. The 3,000 denominator reappears, together with the “around half” language familiar from Wikipedia and other online summaries.

September 13, 2017, The Somerville Times, Neil Silberblatt.

Version: essentially the same around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews formulation. The same author’s material moved from an online appearance into print, producing another documentary occurrence without creating another underlying population study.

September 14, 2017, ADL and allied organizations, United States Supreme Court filing.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. The assertion had now reached a brief submitted to the U.S. Supreme Court. This gave a numerical story first located in 1982 newspaper reporting a place in litigation before the nation’s highest court.

March 1, 2018, Public Books, Joshua Benjamin Leavitt.

Version: nearly half of the city’s Jewish population left Atlanta. The geography again changes from Georgia to Atlanta. “Nearly half” replaces “about half,” while leaving the denominator unstated.

March 30, 2018, ADL and allied organizations, Trump v. Hawaii, United States Supreme Court.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. This continued the same historical wording in Supreme Court litigation. It is another example of one inherited assertion being transmitted through multiple legal documents.

August 23, 2018, Atlanta Jewish Times, Logan C. Ritchie.

Version: thousands of Jewish residents escaped the city. The familiar approximately 1,500 statewide departures have again become plural “thousands” associated with Atlanta. The numbers are no longer merely being rounded. The scale and geography have changed.

October 28, 2018, Haaretz, David B. Green.

Version: more than half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This goes beyond the original “half” and “about half.” The proportion has increased to more than half, even though the denominator remains the same 3,000.

February 1, 2019, The Washington Post, Emily Langer.

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews fled the state. This is one of the clearest repetitions of the original numerical formula. Nearly thirty-seven years after the 1982 articles, the same 3,000 and one-half construction was still appearing in a major national newspaper.

March 3, 2019, Deseret News, Sean Reyes and Seth Brysk.

Version: half of Atlanta’s Jewish community fled the state. This repeats the Atlanta variation rather than the original Georgia-wide denominator. The competing Georgia and Atlanta versions were now circulating at the same time.

2020, Taylor Marks, M.A. thesis.

Version: an estimated 3,000 Jews fled Georgia. This is one of the largest numerical mutations in the chain. The original 1982 story said Georgia supposedly had 3,000 Jews total and roughly half, about 1,500, left. Here 3,000 becomes the number who fled.

September 1, 2020, Cairo Review, Jonathan Weisman.

Version: half of Atlanta’s Jewish population simply left. The statewide 3,000 figure disappears and Atlanta again becomes the population unit. The one-half proportion survives even when the denominator and destination are no longer specified.

November 18, 2020, Let’s Go To Court!, Episode 149.

Version: roughly half of the Jewish population there fled. The numerical story had spread into podcast and popular true-crime discussion. The exact population figure is absent, but the one-half formula continues.

January 6, 2021, Hey Alma, Emily Burack.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This is extremely close to the familiar Wikipedia language. It illustrates how durable the original 3,000 and one-half formula had become on the internet.

January 8, 2021, Jewish Journal, Eric Kingsley.

Version: about 3,000 Jews, roughly half the state’s Jewish population, fled the state. This represents the doubled-departure version in full form. If 3,000 equals roughly half of the population, the implied Jewish population is now approximately 6,000, not 3,000. The numerical story has therefore changed substantially from the 1982 formula.

March 2, 2021, Gwendolyn Midlo Hall, Haunted by Slavery.

Version: about half the Jews living in Georgia moved out. The 3,000 denominator is omitted, but the statewide half-population assertion remains. This demonstrates how the fraction can continue circulating independently of the original population figure.

April 28, 2021, American Jewish Archives.

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000-member Jewish community fled the state. This is another near-complete reproduction of the original numerical formula. Its appearance in an archival or historical institution can make the statistic look as though it came from archival demographic research even when the underlying migration count is not identified.

July 12, 2022, Trudy Gold, Lockdown University.

Version: the lynching led to half of Georgia’s Jews leaving. The numerical denominator has disappeared, but the one-half proportion remains. The story had now spread into historical lectures and educational programming.

October 4, 2022, Adam Hochschild, American Midnight.

Version: half the 3,000 Jews living in Georgia left the state. This reproduces the central 1982 arithmetic almost exactly forty years later. A highly visible modern history book therefore gives the figure another generation of circulation.

October 6, 2022, ADL Los Angeles, Eric Kingsley material.

Version: about 3,000 Jews, described as roughly half of the state’s Jewish population, fled the state. This carries forward the doubled version in which 3,000 is no longer the total Jewish population but the alleged number of departures.

October 26, 2022, ADL and allied organizations, Moore v. Harper, United States Supreme Court.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population fled. The Frank example again appears in Supreme Court litigation, several years after the Trump-related briefs. This shows the same historical wording continuing to circulate in unrelated constitutional litigation.

January 12, 2023, No Agenda, Episode 1520.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. The wording closely resembles the Wikipedia formulation and demonstrates transmission into another podcast and online-audio setting.

Winter 2023, American Heritage, Adam Hochschild.

Version: half the 3,000 Jews living in Georgia left the state. Hochschild’s formulation appears again in magazine form. This is another published appearance but comes from the same authorial source family as American Midnight.

April 6, 2023, HISTORY, later updated May 28, 2025.

Version: about half the 3,000 Jews in Georgia left the state. This version returns directly to the familiar 1982 numerical formula. The significance is its continued presence on one of the most widely visited popular-history websites more than forty years after the number first appears in the source trail I have traced.

May 31, 2023, Jewish Journal, Thane Rosenbaum.

Version: half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state altogether. Once again, the original population base and half fraction are repeated as a settled statistic.

October 26, 2023, Davelandblog.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This closely follows the familiar internet formulation. It is another example of the numerical story moving through online historical commentary.

March 19, 2025, The Georgia Sun.

Version: half of Georgia’s Jewry fled the state. The precise denominator disappears, but the half-population assertion remains. More than a century after Frank’s lynching and more than forty years after the earliest numerical version located in this research, the proportion was still being repeated.

September 12, 2025, Chai Channel.

Version: about half the 3,000 Jews in Georgia left the state. This is another direct survival of the 3,000 and one-half formula into contemporary Jewish media.
May 26, 2026, Georgia Public Broadcasting.

Version: about half of Georgia’s Jewish population left the state. The denominator is absent, but the familiar one-half proportion remains. This shows the story continuing in Georgia public-media historical coverage in 2026.

Wikipedia, “Leo Frank,” current version retrieved in 2026.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. Wikipedia remains one of the most visible carriers of the numerical formula. Because so many secondary sites and writers use Wikipedia as a starting point, this wording can continue reproducing itself even when no new demographic research has been done.

Wikipedia, “Lynching in the United States.”

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. The same basic statistic appears on another Wikipedia article, giving the numerical story more than one route into search engines, student research, blogs, and derivative websites.

MurderIndex.

Version: approximately half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This carries the familiar 3,000 denominator and approximately-one-half fraction into an online crime-reference setting.

Langdon Manor Books.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. The same population and fraction appear in bookselling or historical-description material, another example of the number spreading well beyond conventional histories of the case.

HistoryCentral.

Version: nearly half of Georgia’s Jewish population of 3,000 left the state. Here “around” or “about” becomes “nearly,” but the 3,000 denominator remains. The numerical formula survives with only a slight change in qualification.

Stride educational material associated with UJA-Federation of New York.

Version: about half of the Jews in Georgia left the state. The exact 3,000 denominator drops out, leaving the proportion itself. This brings the story into educational material where students can encounter the one-half figure as background history.

Today in Civil Liberties History.

Version: reportedly, half of the Jews living in Georgia left after the lynching. “Reportedly” again indicates transmission from some earlier source rather than a new population study. The half-of-the-population formulation continues even without the 3,000 denominator.

Temple Judah educational handout, preserved through a Doczz mirror.

Version: around half of Georgia’s 3,000 Jews left the state. This is another near-verbatim survival of the familiar formula in educational material. It closes the current list at 70 confirmed publication or documentary appearances, while still representing another repetition of the same numerical family rather than a seventieth independent demographic calculation.

Global News Brief  
1. Bloomberg News: The average U.S. diesel price has surpassed $6 per gallon for the first time, driven by the war with Iran, attacks on Russian refineries and tightening global supplies. Because diesel powers freight transport, deliveries and farm machinery, the record price is raising business costs, threatening further inflation and increasing political pressure ahead of the November midterm elections.

2. AP: Fighting in Yemen escalated as government forces attacked Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea, while the Houthis launched strikes into neighboring Saudi Arabia, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

3. Daily Nation: Kenya’s proposed legal-education regulations would end the Kenya School of Law’s 18-year monopoly by allowing accredited public and private institutions to offer the Advocates Training Programme. The reforms introduce licensing and quality standards, including a KSh5 million accreditation fee, limits on class size and instructor ratios, six months of supervised pupillage and a two-year transitional route for previously excluded law graduates.

4. CNN 5 Things: Accidental ingestion of recreational drugs among young children in the United States surged by more than 3,300% over 25 years, according to a new study, prompting emergency-room doctors to urge parents to store drugs securely and recognize the symptoms of poisoning.

5. CNN: Asian teenagers are widening their academic lead over Western peers, dominating new international reading, mathematics and science rankings, while U.S. students continue to struggle particularly in math. The OECD report links falling global scores to excessive screen time, weaker reading habits and frequent reliance on AI, but notes that countries such as China and Singapore are using AI more effectively by integrating it into teacher guided learning.

6. The Telegraph: Labour mayors are considering a 5% tourist tax despite opposition from hospitality businesses and some Labour backbenchers, who warn that the “anti-growth” policy could deter visitors, eliminate jobs and cost the industry at least £1.6 billion.

7. UN News: UN human-rights investigators warned that renewed violence, political tensions, corruption and impunity in South Sudan are endangering civilians and threatening the country’s planned democratic transition. Following reports of killings, sexual violence, displacement and attacks on aid operations, the commission urged authorities to protect civilians, permit humanitarian access and establish inclusive dialogue and credible safeguards before December’s elections.

8. NY Times: Adults may fear that endless TikTok and Instagram content is causing Gen Z “brain rot,” but digital-culture professor Maxi Heitmayer argues that it does not show young people are becoming less intelligent. Instead, their compulsive scrolling demonstrates how effectively the attention economy is designed to capture and retain users’ focus.

9. Ynet: The Toronto International Film Festival is preparing for protests and increased security around the premiere of Israeli director Avi Nesher’s Our Loves, a drama portraying acts of heroism during the October 7 attacks. The 293-film program also includes works by Israeli director Guy Nattiv, two Palestinian films and several major Oscar contenders, reflecting the festival’s effort to navigate intense political sensitivities surrounding the Middle East.

10. The Athletic: Team USA remained unbeaten at the FIBA Women’s World Cup, sweeping the group stage before crushing Hungary 108–56 to reach its 11th consecutive semifinal. The four-time defending champions set quarterfinal records with 108 points and 31 assists—the first 30-assist quarterfinal performance in tournament history.

11.  Reuters: President Donald Trump dismissed warnings about artificial intelligence as exaggerated and driven by “very negative forces,” arguing that the United States must maintain its lead over China because “whoever wins AI wins.” His remarks came as Anthropic researchers warned of potentially catastrophic risks and leading AI executives—including Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman—supported proposals to slow development and strengthen safeguards.

12. ESPN: No. 2 Georgia routed Western Kentucky 70–20, while No. 3 Notre Dame shut out Rice 52–0. In the marquee matchup, No. 4 Texas scored 21 unanswered fourth-quarter points to edge No. 1 Ohio State 24–23.

13.  Just The News: President Donald Trump said at the Irish Open golf tournament that he plans to lift the U.S. tariff on Irish whiskey.

14. ESPN: Elena Rybakina defeated Aryna Sabalenka to win her first U.S. Open title and second Grand Slam championship of 2026, while Alexander Zverev beat American Ben Shelton for his first U.S. Open crown and second career major, extending the American men’s title drought to 23 years.

LEVC has cut nearly half its workforce and is winding down its current TX taxi as it prepares a replacement model, but declining driver numbers, high financing costs and the end of government plug-in taxi subsidies continue to cloud its future.

Than he married with another woman and with Aisha Bint Abu Bakr, 9 years old, offered by the Aisha father to the prophet. They stayed together until his death, 12 years later. Aisha was  politically active after Muhammad  death.
In a contemporary context, the current president of France Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte Marie-Claude Trogneux have an age gap of about 25 years. Macron was 15 when he met Brigitte  in a school where she was teacher of theater and literature, in Amiens, north of France. She was 40, married, with three sons. Brigitte  was impressed by the intelligence of that adolescent. She was feeling as they were knowing  each other from always. His family didn't want that relationship and sent him to study in Paris. But finally they could marry. He was 29 and she was 54. Macron is the youngest president elected in France until now, at 39 years old.
The great actor Charles Chaplin married Oona O'Neil when he was 54 and she was 18. He was 36 years older than her. When he asked Oona to marry her he said: "Marry me to teach you how to live and you to teach me how to die". She replied:" No Charlie, I will marry you so that you can teach me how to grow up and I will teach you how to be young until the end". It was a happy marriage. They had 8 children and lived together until he died at 88. Oona's father, the four-time Pulitzer Prize winner playwright Eugene O'Neil, was totally against this marriage, and he never spoke to his daughter again.
Georgia O'Keffe, American painter of the first part of XX century, previously married in New York with the pioneering photographer and art dealer Alfred Stieglitz, 24 years older than her, once remained widow, retired in New Mexico, where she met a potter 58 years younger than her, Juan Hamilton. He was her companion, caretaker, and manager. They stayed together until her death, at 98. In the last moments,  his family was taking care of her. Some species of animals live their life together until the end of their life. Royal penguins with an unique sound recognize their couple and live together for the rest of their life. Wolves too. The female put her head in the mouth of the male when she accepts him as her couple. Their union is forever.
May be there is some sort of divine frecuency that put two souls together. May be it is not the numbers of age compatibility which allows two human beings live a true  relationship, but the magic of something deeper related to nature of love.

"The use of the slaves as soldiers with the reward of freedom to those who survived, was strongly advocated during the year. From the beginning of hostilities, they were the laborers on the fortifications in all parts of the Confederacy. At the same early period both the free in considerable numbers enrolled themselves . and slave offered their services, and the former In June, 1861, the Legislature of Tennessee passed an act to authorize the Governor to receive into the military service free persons of color between the ages of fifteen and fifty. Pay and rations were assigned to them. In September one regiment , numbering fourteen hundred, appeared on the field at the review of troops in New Orleans. In February, 1862 , the subject of enrolling the free negroes was discussed in the Legislature of Virginia, and an act passed to provide for their enlistment. The next step was the threat to draft slaves to work on the fortifications when refused to hire them. This was made by Gov. Brown , of Georgia, in November 1862. During the next year they were extensively employed as pioneers, sappers, cooks, nurses, and teamsters, and their employment as a military arm in defence of the country was advocated in Congress. In February, 1864, Congress passed an act making all "male free negroes (with certain exceptions ) between the ages of eighteen and fifty" liable to perform such duties in the army, or in connection with the military defences of the country, in the way of work upon fortifications , or in Government works, etc., as the Secretary of War might from time to time prescribe, and providing them rations, clothing, and compensation. The Secretary of War was also authorized to employ for similar duty twenty thousand male negro slaves, and their owners were guaranteed against escape or death. He was authorized to impress the slaves when he could not hire them; and General Orders No. 32, March 11, 1864, directed the enrollment of the free negroes, and their assignment to the performance of the duties mentioned in the act. Also the employment and impressment of slaves was ordered by the same general orders.

A convention of the Southern Governors next recommended the measure. Other prominent men approved of it, and at the close of the year the arming of the slaves upon certain conditions of service was considered as sure to ensue."
-Appletons' annual cyclopaedia and register of important events v.4 1864 (published 1866)

text:
THE SAGE

THE FORMER RESIDENCE

Boarding Up Our Past 

We were just leaving the Sushi Seki, the world-class Japanese restaurant on Manhattan's Upper East Side when, as we made our way to the parking lot, a distinguished looking fellow accosted my mentor, The Sage.

“My friend, where have you been all these years? I went to your house in Connecticut, only to find it boarded up, and up for sale,” the man gushed.
“That is hardly surprising. I don’t live there anymore. These days, that residence is nothing more than a relic of a distant past,” The Sage replied.

“Son,” the old boy continued as his limousine sped towards The Hamptons, “people often visit our old place of abode in blissful ignorance of the fact that we no longer live there and may, in fact, have long since sold the property. How would you relate that to our life experience?”

I groaned inwardly. Nothing is more tiresome than an intellectual excursion of any sort following a grand gastronomic adventure into Japanese cuisine.
“Sir,” I started, “people will often visit our past more than we do, not knowing that we have long jettisoned that phase of our history to embrace a greater horizon. No longer living in our past, we have, in fact, sold it and used its returns in experience to purchase a new life filled with hopes for a glorious future.”

The Sage stared long and hard at me.
“Do I get the distinct impression that you imply that we do not have to be a prisoner of our past?”
“Absolutely, sir! I do imply that the past simply does not have to define our present, being merely a chapter in the book of our life, and not the entire story.”

“If I understand you, son, although we make mistakes, encounter obstacles, and endure frustrating moments that we would rather consign to the dustbin of history, those despairing moments need not hold us back from entering into the vast vista of success that awaits us at the end of a long journey of honest and noble toil.”
“Sir, it is not for nothing that the world reveres the sheer finesse of your mind,” I said, shamelessly flattering the old boy. 

“Like an old, worn coat, we must discard those stories that no longer serve our best interests. As soon as we discover that our current narrative is becoming our limiting factor, it becomes our obligation to rewrite it to reflect our highest goals, values, and ideals.”
“Son, what if some people continue to view us through the hazy lens of our past?” The Sage asked.
“Sir, it remains their exclusive preserve to think what they will. We must offer such people the gift of our absence since they cannot appreciate our present and presence.”

“Presumably, son, that is because do not require their permission to grow and evolve into the best version of ourselves.”
“Absolutely, sir! Our only obligation is to ourselves; to pick up our pen to script a refreshingly new chapter that is an incontestable reflection of who we are today, and who we wish to be tomorrow. So help us God.”

Yomi Garnett MD
